title: Future-Proof Coding Agents – Bill Chen & Brian Fioca, OpenAI

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is coding agents, the Codex harness, and software-engineering agent systems built on the Codex SDK. Codex is a coding assistant product and the SDK serves as a developer platform for building custom agent products. The discussion covers building coding agent harnesses and deploying them via CLI, IDE plugins, GitHub Actions, and CI/CD pipelines. The content assumes familiarity with agent architecture and SDK integration but is accessible to practitioners rather than researchers. This is a conference talk delivered at an AI Engineer event. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript by the speakers.

summary:
The speakers define a coding agent as three components: a user interface (CLI, IDE, cloud, or background agent), a model (such as GPT-5.1 or Codex Max), and a harness—the interface layer combining prompts and tools in a core agent loop. The harness is the focus because it is fragile and must be rebuilt whenever models change, creating ongoing maintenance burden.

Key harness challenges include model unfamiliarity with custom tools, latency management for thinking models, context window compaction, evolving APIs, and security considerations like sandboxing and permissions. The speakers introduce a framework of intelligence versus habit: intelligence is what a model is good at, while habits are learned behaviors from training such as planning, gathering context, and testing. Over-prompting against a model's habits degrades performance—they observed this when GPT-5 launch users applied prompts designed for other models, causing excessive thoroughness. The lesson is to let models follow their trained behaviors and ask them directly what instructions slowed them down.

Codex is presented as both a model and harness built together, available as a VS Code plugin, CLI, and cloud-callable agent. Its harness manages parallel tool calls, thread merging, sandboxing, compaction, MCP plumbing, and image compression. A notable capability is a computer use agent for the terminal, enabling Codex to accomplish any task expressible via command line, not just coding—examples include organizing desktop photos and analyzing CSV files.

Emerging patterns show Codex used as an SDK (TypeScript, Python, GitHub Action, agents SDK with MCP connectors). The harness-as-abstraction-layer pattern lets teams avoid re-optimizing prompts and tools per model upgrade. The speakers push back against the wrapper characterization, arguing the abstraction layer delivers real infrastructure value. Agents can write their own tool connectors on the spot, replacing what professional services teams previously did manually.

Partner integrations demonstrate real adoption: GitHub used the SDK to directly integrate with Codex; Zed wrapped Codex inside a layer with an IDE interface, letting them focus on building the best code editor while OpenAI handles the agent infrastructure. The Cursor team customized performance by aligning their tools to the model's training distribution and aligning their harness with the open-source Codex CLI implementation, which is publicly available for forking. The Codex SDK can also control Codex in CI/CD pipelines or as an agent interacting with custom agents.

Looking forward, the speakers emphasize building where models are going. Models will improve, handle longer-horizon unsupervised tasks, and raise the trust ceiling. The future involves sprawling codebases, non-standard libraries, closed-source environments, and matching existing practices. The SDK will evolve to support model learning from experience, avoiding repeated mistakes, and providing more terminal-based problem-solving surface area.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & The State of Coding Agents
sections.summary: Bill and Brian introduce themselves as OpenAI applied AI startup team members focused on coding agents. They frame coding agents as a signal of proximity to AGI, with software engineering as a universal problem-solving medium. The rapid pace of model releases forces constant harness rebuilding, which the talk aims to address.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Coding Agent & The Harness Definition
sections.summary: A coding agent is defined as three parts: user interface, model, and harness. The harness is the interface layer to the model, combining prompts and tools in a core agent loop. It is the focus of the talk because it is fragile and must be rebuilt when models change.

sections.title: Technical Challenges in Building Harnesses
sections.summary: Brian enumerates harness challenges: model unfamiliarity with custom tools, latency of thinking models, context window compaction, evolving APIs, and the complexity of building and maintaining all this infrastructure. Codex Max is noted as handling compaction out of the box.

sections.title: Intelligence vs. Habit: Lessons in Prompt Engineering
sections.summary: The speakers introduce the intelligence-versus-habit framework. Over-prompting against a model's trained habits degrades performance, as seen when GPT-5 users applied prompts from other models. The solution is to let models follow trained behaviors and ask them directly what instructions slowed them down. Building model and harness together provides this knowledge.

sections.title: Deep Dive: Codex as a Harness/Agent
sections.summary: Codex is presented as both model and harness, available as VS Code plugin, CLI, and cloud-callable agent. Its harness manages parallel tool calls, thread merging, sandboxing, permissions, port management, compaction, MCP plumbing, and image compression. A Codex team member emphasized the complexity is greater than expected.

sections.title: Computer Use & Terminal Capabilities
sections.summary: Codex includes a computer use agent for the terminal, enabling any task expressible via command line. Examples include organizing desktop photos and analyzing CSV files for data analysis, extending Codex beyond pure coding tasks.

sections.title: Patterns for Building with the Codex SDK
sections.summary: Emerging patterns show Codex as an SDK usable via TypeScript, Python, GitHub Actions, and agents SDK with MCP connectors. The harness-as-abstraction-layer pattern lets teams avoid per-model re-optimization. The speakers reject the wrapper characterization, emphasizing infrastructure value and differentiation. Agents can write their own API connectors per customer, replacing professional services work.

sections.title: Case Studies: GitHub & Cursor Integration
sections.summary: GitHub used the Codex SDK for direct integration. Zed wrapped Codex inside a layer with an IDE interface, letting them focus on building the best code editor while OpenAI handles agent infrastructure. The Cursor team customized performance by aligning their tools to the model's training distribution and aligning their harness with the open-source Codex CLI implementation, which is publicly available for forking. The SDK can also control Codex in CI/CD pipelines or as an agent interacting with custom agents.

sections.title: Future of Coding Agents & Conclusion
sections.summary: The speakers look forward: models will improve, handle longer-horizon unsupervised tasks, and raise the trust ceiling. The future involves sprawling codebases, non-standard libraries, closed-source environments, and matching existing practices. The SDK will evolve to support model learning from experience and more terminal-based problem-solving. They conclude that harnesses are complicated and hard to maintain, so Codex provides one off the shelf or as open source, letting teams build new things beyond coding while OpenAI maintains the most capable computer agent.
